entry: Art and culture museum in [[Saint Petersburg]], Russia. The museum was founded in 1764 when Empress [[Catherine the Great]] acquired a collection of paintings from the Berlin merchant Johann Ernst Gotzkowsky, and it has been open to the public since 1852. It holds the largest collection of paintings in the world. Its collections comprise over three million items, the numismatic collection accounting for about one-third of them, and only a small part is on permanent display. The collections occupy six historic buildings along the Palace Embankment, including the Winter Palace, a former residence of Russian emperors. The Art Newspaper ranked the museum 10th among the most visited art museums, with 2,812,913 visitors in 2022. Since July 1992, the director has been Mikhail Piotrovsky.

Spanish conquistador and explorer. Cortés led the expedition that resulted in the [[Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire|conquest of the Aztec Empire]], bringing much of present-day [[Mexico]] under the King of Castile. Born into a poor family of nobility in Medellín, Spain, he went to [[Hispaniola]] and later to [[Cuba]], where he received an encomienda. In 1519 he was elected captain of a third expedition to the mainland, which he partly funded. His enmity with the governor of Cuba, Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar, led to an order recalling the expedition, which he ignored. After allying with some Indigenous peoples against others, he overthrew the Aztec Empire and was granted the title Marquis of the Valley of Oaxaca. Cortés wrote to the king asking to be acknowledged for his successes rather than punished for mutiny. Rivalries and inquiries into his conduct reduced his influence by the 1530s, and he died in relative neglect in Spain.

Spanish explorer and conquistador. He took part in expeditions in [[Nicaragua]] and the Yucatán Peninsula and played an important role in Francisco Pizarro's conquest of the Inca Empire in Peru. He is best known for leading the first European expedition deep into what is now the southeastern United States, through Florida, Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, North Carolina, South Carolina, Mississippi and most likely Arkansas. The expedition searched for gold and for a passage to China or the Pacific coast. De Soto is the first European documented as having crossed the [[Mississippi River]]. The expedition began in 1539 with about 600 men. It found no substantial riches or permanent colonies, and roughly half of its men died from combat, disease, starvation and desertion. De Soto died on the banks of the Mississippi River, and sources disagree on whether the site was near present-day Lake Village, Arkansas, or Ferriday, Louisiana.

Abnormal exit of tissue or an organ through the wall of the cavity in which it normally resides. Most hernias involve the [[Abdomen]], especially the [[Groin]], where about 27% of males and 3% of females develop one at some point in their lives. Symptoms include a bulge and pain that often worsens during the day. The main danger is strangulation, which cuts off the blood supply to trapped bowel and requires immediate surgery. Risk factors include [[Smoking]], [[Obesity]], [[Pregnancy]] and [[Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease]]. Groin hernias without symptoms may be watched rather than repaired, but most men eventually need surgery for pain.

Real person or fictional character who combats adversity through courage, ingenuity or strength. In classical heroic epic poetry, the hero fought for glory and honor, often as a semi-divine figure such as [[Achilles]], who fought in the [[Trojan War]]. Classical heroes lived by a flawed personal code of honor and were often foolhardy. Post-classical and modern heroes are defined instead by great deeds or selfless acts for the common good, rather than by the classical goals of wealth, pride and fame. Examples range from mythological figures such as Gilgamesh to historical figures such as [[Joan of Arc]] and [[Giuseppe Garibaldi]], and fictional figures such as [[Superman]], [[Batman]] and [[Spider-Man]]. The antonym of hero is villain.

Greek mathematician and engineer active in [[Alexandria]] during the Roman era. Described as the greatest experimentalist of antiquity, he is known for the aeolipile, a steam-powered device often called Hero's engine, and for a windwheel that was the earliest instance of wind harnessing on land. His work Mechanics described pantographs and a coin-operated machine that dispensed water for ablutions. In mathematics he wrote a commentary on [[Euclid's Elements]] and a work on applied geometry, the Metrica. He is remembered for Heron's formula, which calculates the area of a triangle from the lengths of its sides. Much of his work has been lost, but some survives in manuscripts from the [[Byzantine Empire]] and in Latin or Arabic translations.

Roman Jewish client king of Judea. He is known for colossal building projects, including the rebuilding of the Second Temple in [[Jerusalem]] and the expansion of its base, which includes part of the Western Wall. Herod rose largely through his father's good relations with [[Julius Caesar]], and Mark Antony later named him and his brother Phasael tetrarchs. Despite his successes, including forging a new aristocracy, some historians consider his reign tyrannical, and the Sanhedrin condemned his brutality. Most of what is known of his life comes from the Roman-Jewish historian [[Josephus]], who records the executions of his Hasmonean wife and several sons. The [[Bible|Christian Bible]] describes him as the coordinator of the Massacre of the Innocents. On his death, the Romans divided his kingdom among three of his sons and his sister.

Greek historian and geographer from Halicarnassus (now Bodrum, Turkey), later a citizen of Thurii in Calabria, Italy. He wrote the [[Histories (Herodotus)|Histories]], a detailed account of the [[Greco-Persian Wars]] that also covers the rise of the Achaemenid dynasty of [[Cyrus the Great]]. The work is built around battles such as Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis and Plataea, and it digresses into the cultures, geography and customs of the peoples the Persians encountered. The Roman orator [[Cicero]] called him the "Father of History." Contemporaries criticized his inclusion of legends and fanciful accounts. [[Thucydides]], who wrote on the Peloponnesian War, accused him of making up stories for entertainment, and Herodotus replied that he reported what he could see and what he was told.

Opioid analgesic, also known as diacetylmorphine or diamorphine, that is synthesized from the dried latex of the opium poppy. It is mainly used as a recreational drug for its euphoric effects, though some countries use it medically to relieve pain, such as during childbirth or a heart attack. It is typically injected into a [[Vein]]. Common side effects include respiratory depression and [[Addiction]], and injection can cause abscesses and infections. Treatment of heroin addiction includes behavioral therapy and medications such as [[Methadone]], and an overdose is treated with [[Naloxone]]. Heroin was first made in 1874 by C. R. Alder Wright.

Long-legged, long-necked freshwater and coastal [[Bird|bird]] of the family Ardeidae. Some species are referred to as egrets or bitterns rather than herons, and egrets do not form a biologically distinct group, being named differently mainly because they are white or have decorative breeding plumes. Herons have long, harpoon-like bills and fly with their necks retracted, unlike [[Stork|storks]], [[Ibis|ibises]], spoonbills and [[Crane (bird)|cranes]]. Some species nest in colonies in trees, while the bitterns use reed beds. The smallest species is usually the dwarf bittern, which measures 25–30 cm, and the largest is the goliath heron, which stands up to 152 cm tall.

Viral infection caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV). HSV-1 more commonly causes infections around the mouth, producing cold sores, while HSV-2 more commonly causes genital infections. Both are transmitted by direct contact with body fluids or lesions, and transmission can occur without symptoms. After infection the virus travels along sensory nerves and resides there lifelong. Outbreaks may be triggered by decreased immune function, stress or sunlight exposure. Genital herpes is a [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infection]] and can spread to an infant during childbirth. Avoiding genital sexual contact is the most effective prevention, and [[Condom|condoms]] decrease the risk. There is no available [[Vaccine]] and no cure, but antiviral drugs such as aciclovir can lessen the severity of episodes. [[Paracetamol]] and topical [[Lidocaine]] may relieve symptoms.

Forage fish of the order Clupeiformes, most of them in the family Clupeidae. Herring often move in large schools near the coast, particularly in shallow, temperate waters of the North Pacific and North [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]], including the [[Baltic Sea]]. Species of the genus Clupea make up about 90% of herring captured in fisheries, and the Atlantic herring, the most abundant, accounts for over half of herring catches. Herring studies were fundamental to the development of fisheries science early in the 20th century. These oily fish have a long history as a food fish, often salted, smoked or pickled, and in the United Kingdom they were known as "silver darlings." Females may deposit from 20,000 to 40,000 eggs, averaging about 30,000, which stick to rock, gravel, sand or [[Algae]] on the sea bed.

Ceremonial county in the East of England, bordering [[Greater London]] to the south. Its largest settlement is Watford, and it has ten districts. The county covers 634 square miles (1,640 km2) and had an estimated population of 1,236,191 in 2024. Much of its undeveloped land is agricultural, and much of the county lies within the Metropolitan green belt. Letchworth has served as the prototype garden city since 1903, and Stevenage became the first town to expand under the New Towns Act 1946. St Albans includes remains of the Roman town of Verulamium. The name Hertford derives from an Anglo-Saxon term meaning deer crossing.

[[International System of Units|SI]] unit of frequency, equal to one cycle or event per second. The hertz (symbol Hz) is used only for periodic events, and its base-unit form is 1/s. It is named after [[Heinrich Hertz]], who provided the first conclusive proof of the existence of electromagnetic waves. Common multiples include kilohertz, megahertz, gigahertz and terahertz. The unit describes periodic waveforms and musical tones, particularly in radio and audio, and the clock speeds of computers. A disc rotating at 60 revolutions per minute has a frequency of 1 Hz. The name replaced "cycles per second" and was adopted by the General Conference on Weights and Measures in 1960.

Scatter plot of stars showing the relationship between their absolute magnitudes or luminosities and their stellar classifications or effective temperatures. It was created independently in 1911 by Ejnar Hertzsprung and in 1913 by Henry Norris Russell, and it represented a major step toward an understanding of [[Stellar evolution|stellar evolution]]. Luminosity increases toward the top of the diagram and surface temperature increases toward the left. Most stars lie along the [[Main sequence]], where stars such as the [[Sun]] spend most of their lives. [[Red giant|Red giants]] and [[Supergiant|supergiants]] lie above it, and [[White dwarf|white dwarfs]] lie below. The diagram is also called a color–magnitude diagram, and observers often use it for stars in clusters, whose members share a single distance.

Ancient Greek poet of the archaic period, traditionally associated with the Boeotian town of Ascra. His surviving works include the Theogony, which traces the origins of the gods and the events that led to the rise of [[Zeus]] to power, and Works and Days, a didactic poem addressed to his brother Perses. Works and Days offers farming advice and moral wisdom, describes the five Ages of Man and includes the myth of Pandora's box. Hesiod's account of being given a laurel staff by the [[Muses]] on Mount Helicon, while pasturing sheep, is among the few personal details in his work. Ancient authors credited him and [[Homer]] with establishing Greek religious customs, and modern scholars regard him as a major source on [[Greek mythology]], farming, early economic thought, [[Astronomy|Archaic Greek astronomy]] and ancient timekeeping.

Landlocked state in Germany, with its capital at Wiesbaden. The largest urban area is [[Frankfurt]] am Main, the country's principal financial centre, and Frankfurt Rhine-Main is Germany's second-largest metropolitan area after Rhine-Ruhr. Hesse is home to the European Central Bank and the Deutsche Bundesbank, both in Frankfurt, and it is one of Germany's richest states in terms of gross regional product per capita. With an area of 21,114.73 sq km and a population of over six million, it ranks among the sixteen German states. The synthetic element hassium, number 108 on the [[Periodic table]], was named after the state in 1997.

English celebrity chef, television personality and food writer. He is regarded as a pioneer of multi-sensory cooking, food pairing and flavour encapsulation, and he came to attention with unusual dishes such as bacon-and-egg ice cream. His restaurant The Fat Duck in Bray, Berkshire, has three Michelin stars and was named the world's best restaurant by the World's 50 Best Restaurants in 2005. He also owns Dinner in London, which has two Michelin stars. Television series, most notably for Channel 4, boosted his public profile. Blumenthal has [[Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder|attention deficit hyperactivity disorder]] and [[Bipolar disorder|bipolar disorder]], and he is an ambassador for the charity Bipolar UK.

Romantic attraction, sexual attraction or sexual behavior between people of the opposite sex or gender. As a [[Sexual orientation|sexual orientation]], it is one of three main categories along with [[Bisexuality]] and [[Homosexuality]], and the term also refers to a sense of identity based on those attractions. Across cultures most people are heterosexual, and heterosexual activity is by far the most common type of sexual activity. It has mostly been viewed as the normative and most socially dominant form of sexual orientation. Scientists do not know the exact cause of sexual orientation, but they theorize that it results from a complex interplay of genetic, hormonal and environmental influences, and they favor biologically based theories. The term was coined alongside homosexual by Karl Maria Kertbeny in 1869.

Pragmatic problem-solving method, often called a mental shortcut or rule of thumb. Heuristics are useful where an optimal solution is impossible or impractical to find, because they speed up the search for a satisfactory one. In [[Cognitive psychology|cognitive psychology]], a heuristic ignores part of the available information to make decisions more quickly, frugally or accurately than more complex methods. Heuristics can create systematic errors. Trial and error is the most fundamental heuristic. Heuristics also guide [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] search algorithms, which estimate the cost of reaching a goal.

American information technology company, founded in 1939 in a one-car garage in Palo Alto, California, by Bill Hewlett and David Packard. The company became an influential part of [[Silicon Valley]].Its first major contract was for an oscillator used in the production of [[Walt Disney]]'s [[Fantasia (1940 film)|Fantasia]]. HP grew into a major maker of [[Personal computer|personal computers]] and [[Printer (computing)|printers]], and it was the world's leading PC manufacturer from 2007 until 2013, when [[Lenovo]] moved ahead. Turmoil from several acquisitions led to declining fortunes in the 2010s. On November 1, 2015, the company split into HP Inc. and Hewlett Packard Enterprise.

Base-16 positional numeral system, also called hex. It uses the digits 0 to 9 and the letters A to F for values ten to fifteen. Because computer hardware is binary and 16 is a power of two, each hex digit represents four bits, or a nibble, so an [[Byte|8-bit byte]] is two hex digits. In mathematics a subscript gives the base, so the decimal value 491 is written 1EB₁₆. In [[C (programming language)|C]] and related languages the prefix 0x is used, as in 0x1EB. In URLs, a space is written %20.

Six-sided [[Polygon|polygon]], from the Greek words for six and corner. The internal angles of any simple (non-self-intersecting) hexagon total 720°. A regular hexagon is equilateral and equiangular, with each internal angle 120°, and it can be divided into six equilateral [[Triangle|triangles]] meeting at its centre. Its side length equals its circumradius, and its longest diagonals are twice the side length. The area of a regular hexagon with side length s is (3√3/2)s², or about 2.598s².

Subphylum of [[Arthropod|arthropods]], named from the Greek for six legs, that comprises the largest clade of arthropods and includes most extant arthropod species. It includes the [[Insect|true insects]] (class Insecta) and the smaller Entognatha, which contains the springtails (Collembola), Protura and Diplura. Hexapods range in length from 0.5 mm to over 300 mm and have a three-part body plan with a thorax bearing three pairs of legs, whereas most other arthropods have more pairs. Insects and springtails are important pollinators, consumers, [[Scavenger|scavengers]] and micropredators in terrestrial environments. Recent studies place hexapods as a subgroup of Pancrustacea, and their closest relatives may be [[Crustacean|crustaceans]].

Lebanese Shia Islamist political party with an active paramilitary wing. It was founded in 1982 by Lebanese Shiite clerics in close cooperation with [[Iran]]. Its 1985 manifesto called for destroying [[Israel]] and expelling Western influence from the region. Hezbollah fought Israeli forces in southern Lebanon until Israel withdrew in 2000, and later fought in the [[Syrian civil war]] alongside the government of [[Bashar al-Assad]]. Its political wing holds 15 seats in the Lebanese Parliament. Some scholars regard it as a resistance movement, while at least 28 countries had designated the organization or its military wing as a terrorist group as of April 2026.
